en: Citra Gāṅgyāyani, intending to perform a sacrifice, chose Āruṇi as his officiating priest. He sent his son Śvetaketu, saying, "Go and conduct the sacrifice for him.

When Śvetaketu had arrived, Citra questioned him while he was seated: "Son of Gautama, is there a world that is secured for me, in which you will establish me? Or else, on whichever path it may be, you shall establish me in that world? He replied, "I do not know this. Come, let me ask my teacher."

Having approached his father, he asked: "He has questioned me thus and thus; how shall I answer? He said: "I too do not know this. We merely go to the assembly after having studied our own Vedic recitation, taking whatever others give us. Come, let us both go. With fuel in hand, he approached Citra Gāṅgyāyani, saying: "I wish to come to you as a pupil. He said to him: "You are worthy of the Brahman, O Gautama, since you have not come here out of pride. Come, I will indeed make it known to you. 1.1.1.

He said: "Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon. By their vital breaths, the bright fortnight is filled; by the dark fortnight, he causes them to be born again. The moon is indeed the door to the heavenly world. Whosoever answers him, him he lets pass through. But whosoever does not answer him, having become rain here, he rains down. He is then born here again as a worm, or a moth, or a fish, or a bird, or a lion, or a boar, or a donkey, or a tiger, or a man, or something else—into those various stations according to his karma and according to his knowledge."
When he has arrived, one asks him, "Who are you? He should reply to him:
"From the wise one, from the fifteenfold progenitor, the seed was brought from the ancestral source."
Therefore, do not impel me toward a male agent;
I have been infused by a male agent into a female matrix.
Being born again and again, he becomes thirteen months by means of the twelfth;
through my father I have found that, indeed, I have found it back.
Therefore, O Seasons, you who are immortal, bring that hither!
"By that truth, by that austerity, I am the season, I am the offspring of the season; who am I? You are I!"—with these words he dismisses him. 1.2.

He comes to the pool Āraṃ; he crosses it by means of his mind. Those who do not know it thoroughly sink into it. He comes to the moments called Yeṣṭihās; they flee away from him. He comes to the river Vijarā; he crosses it by means of his mind alone. There he shakes off his good and evil deeds. His dear relatives obtain the good, and those not dear to him obtain the evil. Just as one driving a chariot might look down at the two wheels of the chariot, so he looks down upon day and night, so upon good and evil deeds, and upon all pairs of opposites. Thus, freed from good and freed from evil, he—knowing Brahman—proceeds toward Brahman itself. 1.4a.

His beloved mental wife, Cākṣuṣī, who is his fitting counterpart, brings flowers; and Ambā, Ambālī, and other Apsarases such as Ambikā and the rest come bringing them. When he approaches in this manner, Brahmā says: "Run toward him! By my glory, will he cross the river Vijarā, or will he not cross it? Five hundred Apsarases go out to meet him: one hundred with garlands in their hands, one hundred with ointments in their hands, one hundred with powders in their hands, one hundred with garments in their hands, and one hundred with fruits in their hands. They adorn him with the adornment of Brahman. Adorned with the adornment of Brahman, he, knowing Brahman, proceeds toward Brahman. 1.4b.

He comes to the Ilya tree; the fragrance of Brahman enters him. He comes to the Sālajya assembly hall; the essence of Brahman enters him. He comes to the Aparājita abode; the splendor of Brahman enters him. He comes to Indra and Prajāpati, the gatekeepers; they flee from him. He comes to the Vibhu-pramita; the glory of Brahman enters him.

She approaches the wise throne-seat (*āsandī*): the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* *sāmans* are its two front feet, the *Śyaita* and *Naudhasa* the two rear feet, the *Vairūpa* and *Vairāja* the two longitudinal side-pieces, and the *Śākvara* and *Raivata* the two cross-pieces. She is wisdom, for by means of wisdom one sees clearly.

He comes to the couch of immeasurable splendor. That is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Its two front feet are the past and the future; its two rear feet are prosperity (*śrī*) and radiance (*īrā*); the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [Sāmans] are its two side-pillars; the *Bhadra* and *Yajñāyajñīya* [Sāmans] are its head-pillars; the *Ṛg* verses and *Sāman* chants are the longitudinal cords; the *Yajus* formulas are the crosswise cords; the stalks of Soma are the mattress; the *Udgītha* is the pillow; and prosperity is the cushion. Upon this the Brahman sits. One who knows this mounts it first with his foot alone. The Brahman asks him: "Who are you? He should reply: 1.5.1–2.10.10 (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7–10) The Brahman says to him: "Who are you? He should answer: "I am you, O venerable sir. The Brahman says: "From whence have you come? He should say: "From the world of the moon. The Brahman says: "Did you know us here? He should say: "Yes, I knew you. The Brahman says: "What is our connection here? He should say: "The *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*. The Brahman says: "What is that one syllable? He should say: "The *Om*. The Brahman says: "Which is the deity of that syllable? He should say: "Breath (*prāṇa*). The Brahman says: "Which is the world of that deity? He should say: "This world, O venerable sir. The Brahman says: "Did you know the ladder? He should say: "Yes, I knew it. The Brahman says: "What is that ladder? He should say: "The *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*. The Brahman says: "Did you know the rungs of that ladder? He should say: "Yes, I knew them. The Brahman says: "What are those rungs? He should say: "Faith is its foundation; sacrifice is its beam; truth is its crossbar; penance is its upright; the *Ātman* is its pinnacle; hope is its cord; glory is its pinnacle-top; the sun is its roof-peak; the sky is its upper covering; the earth is its floor; the quarters are its corners; the intermediate quarters are its intermediate corners; the *Sāman* is its width; the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* are its two side-posts; the *Bhadra* and *Yajñāyajñīya* are its head-posts; the *Ṛg* verses and *Sāman* chants are the longitudinal cords; the *Yajus* formulas are the crosswise cords; the stalks of Soma are the mattress; the *Udgītha* is the pillow; and prosperity is the cushion. This, O venerable sir, is the ladder of the gods. By it the wise ascend to the heavenly world. Those who do not know it, O venerable sir, go by other ladders. The Brahman says: "Welcome, O worthy man! You have found the path of the gods. The Brahman leads him to the hall of the Brahman. There he sees the hall of the Brahman, the lake of the Brahman, the tree of the Brahman, the city of the Brahman, the palace of the Brahman, and the door-keeper of the Brahman. He approaches the door-keeper of the Brahman, who is the *Uktha*. He says to him: "O *Uktha*, open the doors of the Brahman so that I may see the Brahman. He should say: "Who are you, O worthy man? He should say: "I am the *Ṛg*, I am the *Sāman*, I am the *Yajus*; I am the science of the *Ṛg*, I am the science of the *Sāman*, I am the science of the *Yajus*; I am the *Ṛgveda*, I am the *Sāmaveda*, I am the *Atharvāṅgirasa*; I am the history, I am the ancient lore, I am the science, I am the secret doctrine, I am the *Ṛg*, I am the *Sāman*, I am the *Yajus*. Then the *Uktha* opens the doors of the Brahman. He enters. He sees the Brahman sitting on a couch of gold. "I am the season; I am the seasonal product. Born from the womb of space, I am the seed for the wife, the brilliance of the year, the self of every being. You are the self of every being. 'Whoever you are, that am I'—thus [the husband says].
He says to her: 'Who am I?
She should say: 'The Truth.'"

"What is that which is the Real (satya)? That which is other than the gods and the vital breaths (prāṇas) is the Real; but that which is the gods and the vital breaths is "That" (tyam). This is expressed by these words: "the Real. All this is just this much; thus he says to him, "You are all this. "He whose belly is the Yajurveda, whose head is the Sāmaveda, whose form is the Ṛgveda, and who is imperishable—he is to be known as Brahman, the great seer composed of Brahman.
He said to him: "By what means do you obtain my masculine names? "By the vital breath (prāṇa)," he should say. "By what means the neuter ones? "By the mind (manas)."
"By what does one perceive the names of women? "By speech.
"By what does one perceive odors? "By the nose.
"By what does one perceive forms? "By the eye."
"By what [does one perceive] sounds? "By the ear.
"By what [does one perceive] the tastes of food? "By the tongue.
"By what [does one perform] actions? "By the two hands."

"By what [does one experience] pleasure and pain? "By the body. "By what [does one experience] bliss, delight, and procreation? "By the organ of generation. "By what [does one experience] movement? "By the two feet."

"By what are the cognitions and the desires to be known? "One should say: by wisdom alone. He says to him: "Verily, this world of mine is water; that [world] of yours is that [water]. Whosoever knows thus wins that victory which belongs to Brahman, and attains that distinction which belongs to Brahman—whosoever knows thus, whosoever knows thus. 1.7.15.
Thus ends the first chapter.
"Breath is Brahman," so said Kauṣītaki. Of this very breath that is Brahman, the mind is the messenger, the eye is the protector, the ear is the announcer, and speech is the server.

He who knows the mind as the messenger of this breath that is Brahman becomes possessed of a messenger; he who knows the eye as the protector becomes possessed of a protector; he who knows the ear as the announcer becomes possessed of an announcer; and he who knows speech as the server becomes possessed of a server.

To this very breath, which is Brahman, all these deities bring tribute even though it does not ask for it. In the same way, all beings bring tribute to one who knows this, even though he does not ask for it. Its secret teaching (upaniṣad) is: "One should not beg. It is just as if someone, having begged through a village and received nothing, were to sit down and say, "I will not eat what has been given from here. Those who previously refused him are the ones who now invite him; such is the nature of one who does not beg. But those who give food indeed invite him, saying, "Let us give to you. 2.1.10–11. The *prāṇa* is the Brahman. All the gods bring tribute to it without its asking. So do all beings bring tribute to one who knows this, without his asking. Its secret teaching is: "Do not ask. "Breath is Brahman," so Paiṅgya used to say. Of this very breath that is Brahman, speech stands behind it; sight stands behind speech; hearing stands behind sight; mind stands behind hearing; and breath stands behind mind. To this very breath that is Brahman, all these deities bring tribute even though he does not ask for it. In the same way, all beings bring tribute to one who knows this, even though he does not ask for it. His secret teaching (upaniṣad) is: "One should not beg."

It is just as if one were to go begging for alms in a village and, having received nothing, sit down thinking, "I shall not eat what has been given from here. Then those very people who previously refused him invite him; such is the rule for one who does not beg. But the givers of food indeed invite him, saying, "We give to you. (2.2)

Now, therefore, follows the acquisition of a single object of value. If one should desire to acquire a single object of value, on the full moon day, or the new moon day, or during the bright fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion, he should kindle the fire, sweep around it, strew grass around it, and sprinkle water around it; then, bending his right knee, he offers oblations of clarified butter with the dipping-spoon, saying:

"The deity named Speech is the acquirer; may she acquire this for me from that person; to her, svāhā! The deity named Smell is the acquirer; may she acquire this for me from that person; to her, svāhā!"
The deity named Sight is a bestower of boons; may she grant this to me from that person. To her, svāhā!
The deity named Hearing is a bestower of boons; may she grant this to me from that person. To her, svāhā!
The deity named Mind is a bestower of boons; may she grant this to me from that person. To her, svāhā!
"The deity named Prajñā (Wisdom) is a bestower of boons; may she grant this for me from that person. To her, svāhā!

Then, having smelled the fragrance of smoke and having rubbed his limbs with an anointing of clarified butter, he should go forth while restraining his speech and state his purpose, or send a messenger; thus they will surely obtain it. 2.3.

Now, therefore, follows the divine *smara* (remembrance). For one whom he desires to become dear, or for whomsoever—whether it be a man, a woman, or many—it is on a single festival day that he offers these oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of this very procedure:
"I offer your speech into me, O [Name], svāhā! I offer your breath into me, O [Name], svāhā!"
I offer your eye into me, O [Name], svāhā! I offer your ear into me, O [Name], svāhā!
I offer your mind into me, O [Name], svāhā!
"I offer my wisdom into you; [Name], svāhā!

Then, having smelled the fragrance of the smoke and having anointed his limbs with the smear of clarified butter, he should go forth in silence. If he wishes to attain physical contact, he should stand even against the wind while conversing; thus he becomes truly beloved and people indeed remember him. 2.4.12–13.

Now, therefore, they speak of the internal Agnihotra known as the Prātardana sacrifice of self-restraint. For as long as a person speaks, he is not able to breathe; at that time, he offers the breath into speech. And as long as a person breathes, he is not able to speak; at that time, he offers speech into the breath.

These two offerings, which are infinite and immortal, he offers continuously while waking and while sleeping. Now, those other offerings which are finite consist indeed of ritual action (*karman*). Knowing this, the ancients did not perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice. 2.5.

"Uktha is Brahman," so said Śuṣkabhr̥ṅgāra. One should meditate upon it as the *Ṛc*. All beings indeed pay homage to him for his preeminence. One should meditate upon it as the *Yajus*. All beings indeed join themselves to him for his preeminence. One should meditate upon it as the *Sāman*. All beings indeed bow down to him for his preeminence.

One should venerate that as "Prosperity. One should venerate that as "Fame. One should venerate that as "Radiance. Just as this [Veda] becomes the most prosperous, the most famous, and the most radiant among sacred texts, even so does one who knows this become the most prosperous, the most famous, and the most radiant among all beings.

The Adhvaryu priest constructs this self consisting of sacrificial work (karmamaya) pertaining to the iṣṭi rites; into it he weaves that which consists of the Yajus formulas. The Hotṛ priest weaves into that which consists of the Yajus that which consists of the Ṛc verses; the Udgātṛ priest weaves into that which consists of the Ṛc that which consists of the Sāman chants. This very self belongs to the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā); and he who knows this becomes the very self of Indra. 2.6.2.6.

Now, therefore, there are three modes of worship belonging to Sarvajit Kauṣītaki. Sarvajit Kauṣītaki used to worship the rising sun as follows: having arranged the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and brought water, he pours it out three times into a water-vessel, saying, "Thou art the separator; separate my evil. By this same procedure, when [the sun] is at the meridian, he says, "Thou art the upward-separator; separate my evil from me. By this same procedure, when [the sun] is setting, he says, "Thou art the uniter; unite my evil [with itself]. Whatever evil he has committed during the day and night, that he thereby unites [and removes].
In the same way, one who knows this worships the sun with this very procedure; whatever evil he does by day or by night, he removes it. 2.7.
Then, on every new moon day, he should worship the moon while it is visible in the west according to this same procedure; or he throws green grass [into the fire] with the verse:
"My heart, well-kindled, rests upon the moon;
I consider myself to know that—may I not weep over the misfortune of a daughter."
"For from this [fire], the offspring do not depart before their time"—thus for one who has a son born. Now, for one whose son is not yet born:
"Swell up! Let it come together unto thee; let thy milks and thy strengths come together."

Having murmured these three verses beginning with, "The stalk which the Ādityas cause to swell," he says: "Do not swell by means of our breath, progeny, or cattle; rather, swell by means of the breath, progeny, and cattle of him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, saying, "I turn according to the turning of Indra; I turn following the turning of the Āditya," he turns around following his right arm. 2.8.
Then, on the full moon day, he should worship the moon while it is still visible in the east, following this same procedure:
"O King Soma, you are far-sighted; you are Prajāpati with five faces. The Brāhmaṇa is one of your faces; with that face, you eat the kings."
By that mouth, make me an eater of food.
You have one mouth; by that mouth you eat the subjects; by that mouth, make me an eater of food.
The hawk is one of your mouths; with that mouth you eat birds; with that mouth, make me an eater of food.
Agni is one of your mouths; with that mouth you eat this world.
By that mouth, make me an eater of food.
You have a fifth mouth; by that mouth you eat all beings—by that mouth, make me an eater of food.
"Do not decline by means of our life, progeny, or cattle;
let him who hates us and whom we hate decline by means of his life, progeny, and cattle."
"I turn following the turning of the divine; I turn following the turning of the sun," saying this, he turns around his right arm.
Then, having reflected, he should touch his wife's heart with [the mantra]:
"O thou of beautiful hair, that which is thy heart resting within Prajāpati, by that [power] which thou art mistress of immortality, mayest thou not suffer the misfortune of childlessness. Thus.
For its offspring do not perish before it. ||2.10||
Then, having returned from his journey, he should kiss his son’s head, saying:
"From limb by limb you arise; from the heart you are born.
You are my very self, O son; live for a hundred autumns."
He gives him a name:
"Be a stone, be an axe, be invincible gold; O son, you are indeed splendor by name; live for a hundred autumns! Thus he says.
He takes his name. Then he encircles him:
"With that by which Prajāpati encompassed his offspring for their safety—with that I encircle you."
"Here he is! Then, he murmurs into his right ear: "Bestow upon him, O Maghavan, O Ṛjīṣin! Into the left ear: "O Indra, bestow the most excellent riches! And:
"Do not cut him off, do not let him falter; may he live for a hundred autumns of life."
Live, my son! I kiss your head in your name.
He should smell his head three times, saying, "This one.
He should murmur over his head three times, saying, "I murmur over you with the lowing of cows. || 2.11 ||

Now, therefore, follows the divine *parimara* (the dying around). This Brahman indeed shines when the fire blazes; it dies when it does not blaze. Its brilliance goes to the sun, its vital breath (*prāṇa*) to the wind. This Brahman indeed shines when the sun is seen; it dies when it is not seen. Its brilliance goes to the moon, its vital breath to the wind. This Brahman indeed shines when the moon is seen; it dies when it is not seen. Its brilliance goes to lightning, its vital breath to the wind. This Brahman indeed shines when lightning flashes; it dies when it does not flash. Its brilliance goes to the quarters, its vital breath to the wind. All these deities, having entered the wind and merged into the wind, do not perish; from that very source they rise up again.
Thus with reference to the deities. Now, with reference to the self. 2.12.

This Brahman indeed shines when one speaks with speech; then it dies when one does not speak. Its radiance passes into the eye, and its vital breath into the breath. This Brahman indeed shines when one sees with the eye; then it dies when one does not see. Its radiance passes into the ear, and its vital breath into the breath. This Brahman indeed shines when one hears with the ear; then it dies when one does not hear. Its radiance passes into the mind, and its vital breath into the breath. This Brahman indeed shines when one thinks with the mind; then it dies when one does not think. Its radiance passes into the breath, and its vital breath into the breath. All these deities, having entered the breath and merged into the breath, do not perish; therefore, they emerge from it once again.

Therefore, if indeed both mountains—the southern and the northern—should rush toward one who knows this, desiring to crush him, they would not be able to strike him down. Rather, those who hate him and those whom he himself hates, they alone perish around him.

Now, therefore, follows the attainment of the supreme good. These deities, indeed, while disputing among themselves as to who was the best, departed from this body. Thereupon, it remained like a piece of wood. Then speech entered it; yet it spoke with speech, but remained as if lifeless. Then sight entered it; it spoke with speech and saw with sight, but remained as if lifeless.

Then it entered that ear. While speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and hearing with the ear, it remained as if lifeless. Then it entered that mind. While speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind, it remained as if lifeless.
Then the vital breath (prāṇa) entered it; thereupon, it stood up from that very moment.

Indeed, all these deities, having recognized the supreme excellence in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and having fully merged with the vital breath which is the self of intelligence (*prajñātman*), departed together with all of them from this body. Having entered into the wind and become of the nature of space (*ākāśātman*), they went to the heavenly world (*svar*).

In the very same way, one who knows this, having recognized the supreme good in the vital breath (prāṇa) and having fully realized the vital breath as the conscious self (prajñātman), departs from this body together with all these [elements]. Having entered the wind and become of the nature of space (ākāśātman), he goes to the light. He goes to where those gods are; having reached that, he becomes immortal, just as the gods are immortal—he who knows thus. 2.14.

Now, therefore, they explain the "Transmission from Father to Son. When the father is about to depart for the next world, he calls his son. Having strewn the house with fresh grass, kindled the fire, and placed a water-pot together with a vessel nearby, the father lies down covered by an unwashed garment. The son approaches and lies down upon him, touching his own sense organs to those of the father. Or rather, he should transmit [the knowledge] to him while he is seated and facing him. Then he hands it over to him: "I place my speech in you," says the father; "I place your speech in me," says the son.
"May I place my breath in you," says the father. "I place your breath in me," says the son.
"May I place my sight in you," says the father. "I place your sight in me," says the son.
"May I place my hearing in you," says the father. "I place your hearing in me," says the son.
"May I place my food-flavors in you," says the father. "I place your food-flavors in me," says the son.
"May I place my actions in you," says the father. "I place your actions in me," says the son.
"May I place my pleasures and pains in you," says the father. "I place your pleasures and pains in me," says the son.

"May I place joy, delight, and progeny in you," says the father. "May I place joy, delight, and progeny in you," says the son. "May I place 'it' in you," says the father. "May I place 'it' in you," says the son.
"May I place my mind in you," says the father. "May you place your mind in me," says the son.
"May I place my wisdom in you," says the father. "May you place your wisdom in me," says the son.
Or, if he should be one who speaks in a whisper, he should say it all in brief.

"I place my vital breaths in you," says the father. "I place your vital breaths in me," says the son. Then, turning to the right, he goes out toward the east. The father addresses him with the mantra: "May glory, spiritual luster, and fame attend you. Then the other [the son] looks back over his left shoulder, having either covered himself with his hand or with the hem of his garment, saying: "May you attain the heavenly worlds and all desires."

If he recovers, the father may live under the authority of his son or go abroad; but if he should die, they should complete for him that which is to be completed, in the manner in which it is to be completed—in the manner in which it is to be completed. 2.15.
[Thus ends the second chapter.]

Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through battle and through his manly prowess. Indra said to him, "Pratardana, choose a boon. Pratardana replied, "Choose for me yourself that which you consider most beneficial for a human being. Indra said to him, "One who is superior does not choose a boon for one who is inferior; you choose it yourself. Pratardana said, "I am indeed inferior. Nevertheless, Indra did not depart from the truth, for Indra is Truth itself.

Indra said to him: "Know me alone! This indeed I consider the most beneficial for a human being—that he should know me. I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ; I delivered the Arurmaghas and the Yatīs to the hyenas; transgressing many compacts, I struck down the followers of Prahlāda in heaven, the Paulomas in the intermediate space, and the Kālakāñjas on earth. Not even a single hair of mine was harmed therein."

He who knows me—indeed, not a single hair of his is harmed by any deed whatsoever: neither by theft, nor by the killing of an embryo, nor by the murder of a mother, nor by the murder of a father; the dark stain does not depart from the face of one who has committed evil, [but for him it does]. 3.1.

He said: "I am the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the conscious self (*prajñātman*). Worship me as life (*āyus*) and immortality (*amṛta*). Life is the vital breath, and the vital breath is life. For as long as the vital breath dwells in this body, so long is there life. Indeed, by means of the vital breath one attains immortality in this world, and by means of consciousness, true resolve. He who worships me as life and immortality reaches a full lifespan in this world and attains immortality and imperishability in the heavenly world."

Regarding this, some say that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) indeed become unified. For no one would be able to make known a name with speech all at once, nor form with the eye, nor sound with the ear, nor meditation with the mind. Having become unified, each one of these makes all of them known. When speech speaks, all the vital breaths speak after it; when the eye sees, all the vital breaths see after it; when the ear hears, all the vital breaths hear after it; when the mind meditates, all the vital breaths meditate after it; when the breath breathes, all the vital breaths breathe after it.
"So it is indeed," said Indra; "but there is indeed a higher good regarding the vital breaths. 3.2.132.

"One lives bereft of speech, for we see the mute; one lives bereft of sight, for we see the blind; one lives bereft of hearing, for we see the deaf; one lives bereft of mind, for we see infants; one lives with an arm cut off, one lives with a leg cut off—for thus indeed we see.

But, verily, it is *prāṇa* alone, as the conscious self (*prajñātman*), which, having taken hold of this body, makes it stand up. Therefore, one should worship this very *prāṇa* as the *uktha*. This is the attainment of all things in *prāṇa*.

That which is breath is indeed wisdom; that which is wisdom is indeed breath. This is the proof of it, this is the knowledge of it: when a person is asleep and sees no dream whatsoever, then they become one in this very breath. Then speech enters into it together with all names; sight enters into it together with all forms; hearing enters into it together with all sounds; and the mind enters into it together with all thoughts. When he awakens, just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so from this Self the vital breaths go forth each to its own place, from the breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds.

This very vital breath (*prāṇa*), being the conscious self (*prajñātman*), having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise up. Therefore, one should worship this alone as the *uktha*. This is the attainment of all things within the vital breath.

From him, speech emits all names; by means of speech, he attains all names. From him, the sense of smell emits all odors; by means of the sense of smell, he attains all odors. From him, the eye emits all forms; by means of the eye, he attains all forms. From him, the ear emits all sounds; by means of the ear, he attains all sounds. From him, the mind emits all thoughts; by means of the mind, he attains all thoughts. This is the attainment of all things within the vital breath (*prāṇa*). That which is the vital breath is wisdom (*prajñā*); that which is wisdom is the vital breath. For these two dwell together in this body and depart together from it.
Now, indeed, we shall explain how all beings become one in this wisdom. 3.4.

Speech alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituent named "name" is laid out. The sense of smell alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituent named "odor" is laid out. The eye alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituent named "form" is laid out. The ear alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituent named "sound" is laid out. The tongue alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituent named "taste of food" is laid out. The two hands alone are one limb drawn out from her; beyond them, the elemental constituent named "action" is laid out. The body alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituent named "pleasure and pain" is laid out. The organ of generation alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituent named "bliss, delight, and procreation" is laid out. The two feet alone are one limb drawn out from her; beyond them, the elemental constituent named "motion" is laid out. Intelligence alone is one limb drawn out from her; beyond it, the elemental constituents named "thoughts, objects of cognition, and desires" are laid out. (3.5)

Having mounted speech by means of wisdom, one attains all names through speech. Having mounted the sense of smell by means of wisdom, one attains all odors through the sense of smell. Having mounted the eye by means of wisdom, one attains all forms through the eye. Having mounted the ear by means of wisdom, one attains all sounds through the ear. Having mounted the tongue by means of wisdom, one attains all tastes of food through the tongue. Having mounted the two hands by means of wisdom, one attains all actions through the two hands. Having mounted the body by means of wisdom, one attains pleasure and pain through the body. Having mounted the organ of generation by means of wisdom, one attains bliss, delight, and procreation through the organ of generation. Having mounted the feet by means of wisdom, one attains all movements through the feet. Having mounted the intellect by means of wisdom alone, one attains the objects to be known and desires through wisdom alone. (3.6)

For speech, deprived of consciousness (prajñā), could not make known any name; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that name. For the sense of smell, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any odor; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that odor. For the eye, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any form; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that form. For the ear, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any sound; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that sound. The tongue, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any taste of food; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that taste of food. For the two hands, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any action; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that action. For the body, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any pleasure or pain; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that pleasure or pain. For the organ of generation, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any pleasure, delight, or procreation; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that pleasure, nor delight, nor procreation. For the two feet, deprived of consciousness, could not make known any movement; one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive that movement. Indeed, no cognition would be accomplished if consciousness were deprived [of its object], nor would anything to be cognized be made known. (3.7)

One should not seek to understand speech; one should know the speaker. One should not seek to understand smell; one should know the smeller. One should not seek to understand form; one should know the seer. One should not seek to understand sound; one should know the hearer. One should not seek to understand the taste of food; one should know the knower of the taste of food. One should not seek to understand action; one should know the agent. One should not seek to understand pleasure and pain; one should know the knower of pleasure and pain. One should not seek to understand bliss, nor delight, nor procreation; one should know the knower of bliss, delight, and procreation. One should not seek to understand the mind; one should know the thinker.

These, indeed, are the ten elements of being (bhūtamātrā) with reference to wisdom (prajñā), and the ten elements of wisdom (prajñāmātrā) with reference to being. For if there were no elements of being, there would be no elements of wisdom; and if there were no elements of wisdom, there would be no elements of being. Indeed, from either one alone, no form whatsoever could be established.
Thus ends the third chapter.

Now, Gārgya Bālāki was indeed a learned man who had traveled far and wide; he lived among the Uśinaras, the Satvats, the Matsyas, the Kurus, the Pañcālas, the Kāśis, and the Videhas. He went to Ajātaśatru, the king of Kāśi, and said, "I shall tell you about Brahman. Ajātaśatru said to him, "We will give you a thousand [cows] for such a speech—for people run about crying, 'Janaka! Janaka! (4.1)

"In the sun is the Great; in the moon, food; in lightning, brilliance; in thunder, sound; in the wind, Indra Vaikuṇṭha; in space, the Full; in fire, the Conqueror of Enemies; in the waters, Truth"—thus with respect to the deities. Now, with respect to the self: "In a mirror, the reflection; in a shadow, the double; in an echo, the Asura; in sound, Death; in sleep, Yama; in the body, Prajāpati; in the right eye, Speech; in the left eye, Truth. 4.2.

Bālāki said: "The person who is there in the sun, that very one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as the pre-eminent, the head of all beings. He who meditates upon him thus becomes pre-eminent, the head of all beings. (4.3)

Bālāki said: "The person who is there in the moon, that very one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as the Great One, clad in white, King Soma, the self of food. He who meditates upon him thus becomes the self of food. (4.4)

Bālāki said: "The person who is in the thunder—him indeed I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as the Self of sound. He who meditates upon him thus becomes the Self of sound. (4.6)

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the wind, him indeed I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the unconquered army. He who meditates upon him thus becomes victorious, unconquerable, and a conqueror of others' armies. (4.7)

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the fire—that very one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as 'the overcomer. He who meditates upon him as such indeed becomes an overcomer among others. (4.9)

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the waters, him indeed I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as the self of truth. He who meditates upon him thus becomes the self of truth. This is with respect to the divine; now, with respect to the self. 4.10.

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the mirror—that very one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as 'the Counterpart' (Pratirūpa). He who meditates upon him as such, a counterpart indeed is born to him in his offspring, and not one who is not a counterpart. ||4.11||

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the shadow—that is the one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as the 'Inseparable Companion' (Anapaga), the Second. He who meditates upon him in this way finds a companion; for he becomes possessed of a companion. ||4.12||

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the echo—that indeed I worship. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I worship him rather as 'the Spirit' (asuḥ). He who worships him thus does not fall into confusion before his time. ||4.13||

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in sound—that is the one I venerate. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I venerate him rather as Death. He who venerates him thus does not depart before his time. ||4.14||

Bālāki said: "The person who, when asleep, moves about in dreams—that is the one I worship. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not talk to me about that one! I worship him as Yama, the King. Whoever worships him thus, everything here is indeed brought under his control for his supremacy. (4.15)

Bālāki said, "The person who is here in the body—that is the one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him, "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as Prajāpati (the Lord of Creatures). He who meditates on him in this way is procreated with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan. ||4.16||

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the right eye—that is the one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about that one! I meditate upon him as the Self of speech, the Self of fire, and the Self of light. Whoever meditates upon him in this way becomes the Self of all these. (4.17)

Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the left eye—that is the one I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him! I meditate upon him as the Self of truth, the Self of lightning, and the Self of splendor. Whoever meditates upon him in this way becomes the Self of all these. 4.18.

Thereupon Bālāki became silent. Ajātaśatru said to him, "Is that all, Bālāki? "That is all," replied Bālāki. Ajātaśatru said to him, "Truly, you have been deceiving me! Let me tell you about Brahman. O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these persons, and whose work this is—he indeed is the one who ought to be known."

Then Bālāki, with a sacrificial fuel-stick in his hand, approached him, saying, "I come to you as a pupil. Ajātaśatru said to him, "I consider it a form of acting contrary to the natural order that a Kṣatriya should initiate a Brāhmaṇa. Come, I will simply make it known to you. Taking him by the hand, he went forth. They came upon a man who was asleep. Ajātaśatru addressed him, "O Great One, clad in white, King Soma! But he remained lying down. Then he nudged him with a staff, and he rose up at once.

Ajātaśatru said to him: "Bālāki, where was this person lying when he was asleep? Where did he go to be there? From where did he come back? Bālāki did not know this. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Bālāki, as to where this person was lying when he was asleep, where he went to be there, and from where he came back—there are channels called *hitā* that extend from the heart to the pericardium. As fine as a hair split a thousandfold, so minute they remain, filled with white, black, yellow, and red [fluids]. When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, he is then in those [channels]. 4.19.

Then, in this very breath (*prāṇa*), they all become one. Then speech enters into it together with all names; sight enters into it together with all forms; hearing enters into it together with all sounds; and the mind enters into it together with all thoughts. When he awakens, just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so from this Self (*ātman*) the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) emerge according to their respective stations, from the breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds.

This very vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the conscious self (*prajñātman*), has entered this body as its self, down to the hairs and the nails. Just as a razor is placed in a razor-case, or as a bird is in its nest, even so has this conscious self entered this body as its self, down to the hairs and the nails. These selves settle upon this self, just as one's own subjects settle upon their lord. Just as the lord enjoys himself with his subjects, or as the subjects serve the lord, even so does this conscious self enjoy itself through these selves, and even so do these selves serve this self.

As long, indeed, as Indra did not recognize this Self, so long were the Asuras superior to him. When he recognized it, then, having slain the Asuras and conquered them, he attained the preeminence, sovereignty, and overlordship of all the gods. In the same way, one who knows this, having struck away all evils, attains the preeminence, sovereignty, and overlordship of all beings—whosoever knows this, whosoever knows this. 4.20.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Thus ends the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.
